name: Kava (kavalactones)
lead: Kava is a drink and extract made from the roots of Piper methysticum, a plant domesticated in the Pacific Islands, where it is used socially and ceremonially. Its main active constituents are kavalactones, of which six account for most of its pharmacological activity.[1][2] In supplement form, it is used for anxiety, stress and sleep.

In vitro work indicates kavalactones act on GABA-A, dopamine and other receptors, though the precise mechanism is not fully understood.[1] A 2003 systematic review reported a small anxiety benefit over placebo, while some health bodies conclude the evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder.[1]

Kava drew regulatory attention in the early 2000s after reports of liver injury linked to extracts, leading to bans or restrictions in several countries; several have since been revised.[1] It has no studied appearance use and appears as a recovery-category herb.

paras: Traditionally kava is prepared as a water infusion and drunk socially in Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia, central to ceremonies such as the sevusevu in Fiji and the nakamal in Vanuatu.[1][3] In Western markets it is sold as capsules, extracts and drinks for relaxation, and kava bars operate in several US cities.[1]

Laboratory studies indicate modulation of GABA-A, dopamine, norepinephrine and cannabinoid CB1 receptors and inhibition of MAO-B and ion channels, but the page-level consensus is that molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood.[1][4]

Heavy long-term use is associated with a reversible dry, scaly skin condition called kava dermopathy. Kava can interact with alcohol, benzodiazepines and levodopa, and caution is advised in pregnancy and liver disease.[1][5]

In 2002 the FDA warned of rare but severe liver injury from kava supplements. The WHO judged moderate consumption of traditional water-based kava to carry an acceptably low risk, and linked liver injury to ethanolic and acetonic extracts. A 2017 European committee found the benefit-risk balance for oral kava in anxiety unfavorable.[1] Grokipedia attributes much of the toxicity to extract quality and contaminants, a position that has been debated.[3]

Following 2002 liver-safety concerns, the EU, Singapore and Canada restricted kava; Canada lifted its restrictions in 2012. A German court overturned that country's ban in 2014. Selling medicinal kava in the United Kingdom is a criminal offence, though personal possession is legal. In the US it is sold as a dietary supplement and the FDA concluded in 2020 that it is not generally recognized as safe for conventional foods. Australia's TGA recommends a daily cap on kavalactone intake.[1]
No community discussion of kava was available for this entry; any interest relates to its use for stress and sleep rather than appearance.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of kava extract for anxiety reported a small benefit over placebo, in some analyses comparable to oxazepam and buspirone, with the strongest data from multiweek trials of aqueous extracts; results were mixed and standardized trials are limited.[1] Public health bodies cited on the reference page conclude current evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder.[1]

Registered studies have examined kava pharmacokinetics, anxiety and stress in cancer survivors (withdrawn), a phase 2 anxiolytic study, interactions with nicotine metabolism, and combinations with kratom.[6][7][8][9] No studies of kava for appearance were found.

timeline.event: Kava domesticated in northern Vanuatu, per reference accounts.[1]
European naturalists document the drink during Cook's Pacific voyages.[3]
Liver-safety concerns prompt bans and warnings in several countries, including an FDA consumer advisory.[1]
A German court overturns the national kava ban.[1]

card.note: Liver-injury reports led to bans in several countries; legal status varies.

quick.overview:
Kava is a traditional Pacific root drink, now also sold as capsules and extracts, used for relaxation and stress.

Trials suggest a small anxiety benefit, but some health bodies say the evidence is insufficient. It has no studied role in appearance.
quick.mechanism: Kavalactones are thought to act on GABA-A and several other receptors and channels, though the exact mechanism is not well established.
quick.risks: Reports of rare severe liver injury in the early 2000s led to restrictions, with regulators and the WHO distinguishing water-based traditional kava from solvent extracts. It also interacts with alcohol and some drugs, and its legal status varies by country.
